chunks: As for the report narrated by Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-'Abbas, from Abu Shu'ayb, from 'Imran ibn Humran — that he heard a righteous servant (AS) say:
«Whoever falls asleep while sitting, not intentionally seeking sleep, then no wudu is required of him.»

key_terms.النَّوْمَ: sleep — an established nullifier of wudu in Islamic jurisprudence; this hadith carves out an exception for unintentional dozing
key_terms.عَبْداً صَالِحاً: righteous servant — Shia euphemistic epithet for an Imam, used to conceal identity; most likely Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS)
key_terms.وُضُوءَ: wudu — ritual ablution prerequisite to salat; one of the primary acts of taharah
key_terms.يَتَعَمَّدُ: intentionally seeks — the criterion of deliberate intent that determines whether a legal consequence is triggered

ai.seo_question: Does falling asleep while sitting without intending to sleep break wudu according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Tahdhib al-Ahkam transmits a legal ruling attributed to an Imam referred to by the Shia epithet 'a righteous servant' (عَبْد صَالِح), most likely Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS). The ruling establishes that inadvertent sleep in a seated position — without the intention to sleep — does not nullify wudu, grounding the judgment in the principle that legal obligation is conditioned upon deliberate intent.
